title: Small schematics, written as a few lines, simulated through the netlist that is made from them: dividers with values in the marking of parts, an RC filter, a LED and a diode with a resistor, an NMOS inverter and an inverting amplifier

cases.title: Schematic of a voltage divider of 1 kohm and 3 kohm on 10 V
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: a linear solve of a three-node circuit, so only rounding is accepted
cases.source: J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits, the voltage-divider circuit: Vout = Vin R2/(R1 + R2)

cases.title: Divider with the values written in the marking of parts: 2k2 and 6k8 on 10 V
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: a linear solve, so only rounding is accepted; the letter of the marking stands for the decimal point, so 2k2 is 2200 ohm and 6k8 is 6800 ohm
cases.source: IEC 60062, the code for resistance values with a letter in the place of the decimal point (4K7 is 4.7 kilohm), and J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits, the voltage-divider circuit: Vout = Vin R2/(R1 + R2) = 10 x 6800/9000

cases.title: Divider with a capital M in the values (2M2 and 4M7 are 2.2 and 4.7 megohm) on 10 V
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: a linear solve, so only rounding is accepted; the setting upper_m_is_mega of the table of models is on, so a capital M is mega as on the marking of a resistor
cases.source: IEC 60062, the code for resistance values (M for mega), and J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits, the voltage-divider circuit: Vout = Vin R2/(R1 + R2) = 10 x 4.7/6.9

cases.title: Divider whose lower resistor takes its value from an attribute of the part (SIM.VALUE) and not from its text
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: a linear solve, so only rounding is accepted; the attribute is the only place where the value of R2 is a number
cases.source: J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits, the voltage-divider circuit: Vout = Vin R2/(R1 + R2) with R2 = 3 kohm

cases.title: Schematic of a first-order RC low-pass: gain at the corner frequency
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: C = 1/(2 pi R f) for f = 1 kHz, so |H| = 1/sqrt(2) up to the rounding of C
cases.source: J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits, frequency response of the first-order low-pass filter: |H(j w_c)| = 1/sqrt(2) at w_c = 1/(R C)

cases.title: Schematic of a first-order RC low-pass: phase at the corner frequency
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the phase is -arctan(w R C) = -45 degrees up to the rounding of C
cases.source: J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits, frequency response of the first-order low-pass filter: phase = -arctan(w/w_c)

cases.title: Schematic of a LED (generic model of the settings, IS 1e-17 A, n 2) with a 330 ohm resistor on 5 V: voltage across the LED
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: Newton-Raphson stops when the change is below reltol*|v| + vntol twice in a row, which leaves an error of about 1e-5 V on the junction voltage, so 1e-4 V is wider than needed; the LED model is a diode whose IS and n are led_is = 1e-17 and led_n = 2 in config/sim.cfg (values chosen there, not measured on a part), given to the part because its value names no model of the table
cases.source: Shockley ideal diode equation I = Is (exp(Vd/(n Vt)) - 1) with Vt = k T / q (k = 1.380649e-23 J/K, q = 1.602176634e-19 C, T = 300.15 K, the temperature of config/sim.cfg), A. S. Sedra and K. C. Smith, Microelectronic Circuits, the diode forward characteristic; the series circuit Vs = I R + Vd has the closed form I = (n Vt / R) W((Is R / (n Vt)) exp((Vs + Is R) / (n Vt))) - Is with W the principal branch of the Lambert W function (R. M. Corless, G. H. Gonnet, D. E. G. Hare, D. J. Jeffrey and D. E. Knuth, On the Lambert W function, Advances in Computational Mathematics 5, 1996)

cases.title: Schematic of a diode with a model of the table (IS 1e-14 A, n 1) and a 1 kohm resistor on 5 V: voltage across the diode
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: Newton-Raphson stops when the change is below reltol*|v| + vntol twice in a row, which leaves an error of about 1e-5 V on the junction voltage, so 1e-4 V is wider than needed and still far below the 26 mV scale of the junction
cases.source: Shockley ideal diode equation I = Is (exp(Vd/(n Vt)) - 1) with Vt = k T / q (k = 1.380649e-23 J/K, q = 1.602176634e-19 C, T = 300.15 K, the temperature of config/sim.cfg), A. S. Sedra and K. C. Smith, Microelectronic Circuits, the diode forward characteristic; the series circuit Vs = I R + Vd has the closed form I = (n Vt / R) W((Is R / (n Vt)) exp((Vs + Is R) / (n Vt))) - Is with W the principal branch of the Lambert W function (R. M. Corless, G. H. Gonnet, D. E. G. Hare, D. J. Jeffrey and D. E. Knuth, On the Lambert W function, Advances in Computational Mathematics 5, 1996)

cases.title: Schematic of an NMOS inverter with a 1 kohm load, input 0.5 V (below the threshold of 1 V): the transistor is cut off
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the square-law equations are solved by Newton-Raphson, which stops with an error of about 1e-5 V on a 4 V node, so 1e-4 V is wider than needed
cases.source: H. Shichman and D. A. Hodges, Modeling and simulation of insulated-gate field-effect transistor switching circuits, IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits 3(3), 1968, and A. S. Sedra and K. C. Smith, Microelectronic Circuits, the NMOS inverter with a resistive load; with beta = KP W/L = 2e-3 A/V^2, Vov = Vin - VTO and no channel-length modulation, cut-off for Vov <= 0: no drain current, so the output is the supply, 5 V

cases.title: Schematic of an NMOS inverter with a 1 kohm load, input 2.5 V: saturation
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the square-law equations are solved by Newton-Raphson, which stops with an error of about 1e-5 V on a 4 V node, so 1e-4 V is wider than needed
cases.source: H. Shichman and D. A. Hodges, Modeling and simulation of insulated-gate field-effect transistor switching circuits, IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits 3(3), 1968, and A. S. Sedra and K. C. Smith, Microelectronic Circuits, the NMOS inverter with a resistive load; with beta = KP W/L = 2e-3 A/V^2, Vov = Vin - VTO and no channel-length modulation, saturation: Id = beta Vov^2 / 2 = 2.25 mA, Vout = 5 - 2.25 = 2.75 V, which is above Vov = 1.5 V

cases.title: Schematic of an NMOS inverter with a 1 kohm load, input 3 V: triode
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the square-law equations are solved by Newton-Raphson, which stops with an error of about 1e-5 V on a 4 V node, so 1e-4 V is wider than needed
cases.source: H. Shichman and D. A. Hodges, Modeling and simulation of insulated-gate field-effect transistor switching circuits, IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits 3(3), 1968, and A. S. Sedra and K. C. Smith, Microelectronic Circuits, the NMOS inverter with a resistive load; with beta = KP W/L = 2e-3 A/V^2, Vov = Vin - VTO and no channel-length modulation, triode (Vds < Vov): Id = beta (Vov Vds - Vds^2 / 2) with Vds = 5 - 1 kohm Id gives Vds^2 - 5 Vds + 5 = 0, so Vds = (5 - sqrt(5)) / 2, below Vov = 2 V

cases.title: Schematic of an inverting amplifier with 1 kohm and 2 kohm and an op-amp of gain 1e6, input 1 V: output
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the ideal gain is -R2/R1; the finite open-loop gain 1e6 of the model lowers it by the factor 1 + (1 + R2/R1)/A = 1 + 3e-6, which is 6e-6 V at 2 V, so 2e-5 V is wider than that error
cases.source: A. S. Sedra and K. C. Smith, Microelectronic Circuits, the inverting configuration of an ideal op-amp: Vout/Vin = -R2/R1
